content: Hormone therapy (HT) is commonly prescribed to manage menopausal symptoms and has also been used for the prevention and treatment of conditions such as cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and dementia in older women. This updated review evaluates the effects of long-term HT, defined as use for at least one year, on various health outcomes, including mortality, cardiovascular events, cancer, gallbladder disease, fractures, and cognitive function, both during and after cessation of treatment. The review included 22 randomized, double-blinded studies involving 43,637 women, with the majority of data derived from two large, well-conducted trials: the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study (HERS) and the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI). Most participants were postmenopausal women over the age of 60, with some degree of comorbidity. None of the studies specifically focused on perimenopausal women. In relatively healthy postmenopausal women, continuous combined HT (estrogen plus progestogen) was associated with an increased risk of several adverse outcomes. These included coronary events (after one year of use, the risk increased from 2 per 1000 to between 3 and 7 per 1000), venous thromboembolism (after one year, from 2 per 1000 to between 4 and 11 per 1000), stroke (after three years, from 6 per 1000 to between 6 and 12 per 1000), breast cancer (after 5–6 years, from 19 per 1000 to between 20 and 30 per 1000), gallbladder disease (after 5–6 years, from 27 per 1000 to between 38 and 60 per 1000), and death from lung cancer (after 5–6 years of use plus 2–4 years of follow-up, from 5 per 1000 to between 6 and 13 per 1000). Estrogen-only HT also increased the risk of venous thromboembolism (after 1–2 years, from 2 per 1000 to between 2 and 10 per 1000; after 7 years, from 16 per 1000 to between 16 and 28 per 1000), stroke (after 7 years, from 24 per 1000 to between 25 and 40 per 1000), and gallbladder disease (after 7 years, from 27 per 1000 to between 38 and 60 per 1000). However, it reduced the risk of breast cancer (after 7 years, from 25 per 1000 to between 15 and 25 per 1000) and clinical fractures (after 7 years, from 141 per 1000 to between 92 and 113 per 1000). Estrogen-only HT did not increase the risk of coronary events at any follow-up time. In women over the age of 65 who were relatively healthy, continuous combined HT was associated with an increased risk of dementia (after 4 years, from 9 per 1000 to between 11 and 30 per 1000). Among women with pre-existing cardiovascular disease, combined continuous HT significantly increased the risk of venous thromboembolism (after one year, from 3 per 1000 to between 3 and 29 per 1000). Long-term HT use was associated with a significant reduction in fracture risk. This was the only outcome for which strong evidence demonstrated a clear clinical benefit. For example, after 5–6 years of combined HT, the risk of fracture decreased from 111 per 1000 to between 79 and 96 per 1000. Similarly, after 7.1 years of estrogen-only HT, the risk decreased from 141 per 1000 to between 92 and 113 per 1000. There was no strong evidence to suggest that HT has a clinically meaningful impact on the incidence of colorectal cancer. In a subgroup analysis of relatively healthy women aged 50–59, the only significantly increased risk was for venous thromboembolism in those taking combined continuous HT, though the absolute risk remained low (less than 1 in 500). However, the study was not adequately powered to detect other differences in risk within this age group. The overall quality of evidence was moderate, with the main limitation being that only about 30% of participants were aged 50–59 at baseline, which is the age range when women are most likely to consider HT for vasomotor symptoms. The authors concluded that women experiencing intolerable menopausal symptoms may consider short-term use of low-dose HT after weighing the benefits of symptom relief against the small absolute risks, provided they do not have contraindications. HT may not be suitable for women at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, thromboembolic disease (e.g., those with obesity or a history of venous thrombosis), or certain cancers (e.g., breast cancer in women with a uterus). The risk of endometrial cancer with estrogen-only HT in women with a uterus is well-documented. HT is not recommended for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease, dementia, or cognitive decline in postmenopausal women. While HT is effective for preventing postmenopausal osteoporosis, it is generally reserved for women at significant risk who cannot use non-estrogen therapies. There is insufficient data to assess the risks of long-term HT use in perimenopausal women or postmenopausal women younger than 50 years of age.
